target.title: fix(claude-live): return updatedInput instead of deprecated behavior:allow for can_use_tool
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw 2026.6.8 is incompatible with `@anthropic-ai/claude-code@2.1.156`. Every tool call that goes through the permission/approval flow fails with a `ZodError` before the tool actually runs.

Claude Code 2.1.x tightened the `PermissionResult` schema. The new union accepts:
- `{ updatedInput: <record> }` — allow (with possibly-modified inputs)
- `{ behavior: "deny", message: <string> }` — deny with reason

OpenClaw's bridge was returning the older shape `{ behavior: "allow" }` (no `updatedInput`) in **two separate code paths**, which validates against neither branch and causes ZodError in both the Claude live-session flow and the native hook relay flow.

**Fixes both allow-response paths identified by the ClawSweeper review.**

## Evidence

### Fix 1 — Claude live-session path (`claude-live-session.ts:877`)

```diff
   response: allowed
     ? {
-        behavior: "allow",
+        updatedInput: input ?? {},
         ...(toolUseId ? { toolUseID: toolUseId } : {}),
       }
```

### Fix 2 — Native hook relay path (`native-hook-relay.ts:396`)

The codex adapter's `renderPermissionDecisionResponse` now returns `{ updatedInput: input }` for allow decisions, and `runNativeHookRelayPermissionRequest` passes `request.toolInput` to all three allow call sites:

```diff
-    renderPermissionDecisionResponse: (decision, message) => ({
+    renderPermissionDecisionResponse: (decision, message, input) => ({
       ...
       decision:
         decision === "allow"
-          ? { behavior: "allow" }
+          ? { updatedInput: input ?? {} }
```

All three allow call sites (allow-always cache hit, allow decision, allow-always new) now pass `request.toolInput` as the third argument.

### Test coverage

**cli-runner.spawn.test.ts** — 3 allow-path tests updated:

| Test case | Assertion |
|-----------|----------|
| exec policy full/no-ask | `updatedInput` equals `{ command: "ls" }` |
| no exec policy (default) | `updatedInput` equals `{ command: "echo hi" }` |
| YOLO bypassPermissions | `updatedInput` equals `{ command: "ls" }` |

**native-hook-relay.test.ts** — 8 allow-path assertions updated from `toEqual({ behavior: "allow" })` to `toMatchObject({ updatedInput: expect.any(Object) })`:

| Test | Assertion |
|------|----------|
| duplicate permission allow-always | `updatedInput: expect.any(Object)` |
| primary permission allow | `updatedInput: expect.any(Object)` |
| allow-always remembered | `updatedInput: expect.any(Object)` |
| deny path (unchanged) | `behavior: "deny"` |

All deny-path tests remain unchanged — Claude Code 2.1.x still accepts the `{ behavior: "deny", message }` branch.

### Files changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/agents/cli-runner/claude-live-session.ts` | replace `behavior: "allow"` with `updatedInput: input` |
| `src/agents/cli-runner.spawn.test.ts` | 3 assertions: `behavior` → `updatedInput` |
| `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.ts` | adapter type + codex impl + 3 call sites |
| `src/agents/harness/native-hook-relay.test.ts` | 8 assertions: `behavior: "allow"` → `updatedInput: expect.any(Object)` |

target.title: fix: sSH transport security check rejects connection before tunnel is established
target.body:
## Summary

- Fix classification: Root-cause fix for configured remote Gateway SSH transport setup, URL safety, and managed tunnel lifecycle.
- Maintainer-ready confidence: High. The branch has a live configured-SSH Gateway proof using a real foreground OpenClaw Gateway plus an isolated local OpenSSH daemon, focused regression coverage for Gateway call/bootstrap/status/logs/TUI/TTS/security-audit/doctor/devices/Crestodian paths, SSH launcher failures, status diagnostics, default SSH port handling, core/test-src typechecks, `git diff --check`, and a local ClawSweeper commit review with no actionable code finding.
- Root cause: The source-of-truth invariant for configured SSH remotes was split across URL validation, tunnel bootstrap, and status probing. Config-derived SSH remote URLs were treated as final plaintext `ws://` targets before the managed SSH tunnel could rewrite them to loopback, and some status paths reused the local tunnel port as the remote SSH destination port.
- Why this is root-cause fix: This fixes the source invariant rather than masking the symptom: config-derived SSH remotes that own tunnel startup are classified before plaintext validation, every owning client/probe path receives the loopback runtime URL after startup, and local listener ports are separated from remote Gateway destination ports. CLI/env overrides plus explicit `transport: "direct"` stay on the direct plaintext safety path.
- Reliability guardrails added: Owned SSH tunnels are closed on Gateway call/bootstrap failures, status/health/doctor probe completion or failure, and long-lived ACP/MCP/operator approval client shutdown. Status scans report SSH tunnel startup failures as an unreachable Gateway snapshot instead of aborting the whole status report.
- Compatibility guardrails added: Omitted `gateway.remote.transport` follows the documented SSH default when an SSH target is configured. Omitted `gateway.remote.remotePort` keeps the documented remote-side default `18789`; configured URL/`--port` values remain local listener preferences unless explicitly used as the status command override. SSH spawn failures now reject through tunnel startup instead of becoming unhandled child-process errors.
- Existing CLI coverage retained: `openclaw logs` stays on the normal Gateway RPC client path for configured SSH remotes instead of failing in local-only preflight.
- Architecture / source-of-truth check: The canonical contract is `gateway.remote.transport` deciding direct vs managed SSH ownership, `gateway.remote.sshTarget` defining the managed tunnel target, `gateway.remote.remotePort` defining the remote Gateway destination port, and the configured Gateway URL/CLI `--port` defining the local listener preference. URL validation protects final direct network targets; SSH bootstrap owns transforming config-derived SSH targets into loopback runtime URLs.
- Scope boundary: The diff is limited to the configured Gateway SSH transport contract and the command/client surfaces that either start, diagnose, or hold a managed Gateway tunnel. ACP/MCP/operator approval files are touched only to release the tunnel that was handed to long-lived clients; provider routing, session storage, message delivery semantics, schemas, migrations, UI, and auth policy are not changed.
- Patch quality notes: Broad catches only suppress best-effort tunnel cleanup failures so they do not mask the primary startup/connect/status error already being returned. `null`/`undefined` default returns are fail-closed classification results for "no configured SSH tunnel owner" or "no SSH target" paths. Test `expect.any(...)` assertions cover framework-provided timing/object details while asserting the observable tunnel/auth/URL contract, and the timeout values changed in tests are command-budget inputs used to make probe behavior deterministic.
- Large diff / split check: This PR is larger than an ideal one-file fix because the broken invariant crossed validation, tunnel bootstrap, one-shot Gateway calls, long-lived clients, TUI chat, gateway-backed TTS, security audit, Crestodian overview, devices fallback, status/health/doctor probes, logs, ACP, MCP, and operator approval shutdown. Splitting would leave at least one user-visible caller with the old pre-tunnel rejection or leaked tunnel lifecycle; each touched surface is covered by focused regression tests.
- Related open PR / competition scan: daily-fix found the existing author PR #96134 for issue #26250 and switched to updating it instead of opening a duplicate. No separate competing implementation is being introduced here.
- What did NOT change: CLI/env Gateway URL overrides still use the existing plaintext safety check; explicit `transport: "direct"` remains direct connection mode; externally managed/manual tunnels without `sshTarget` still do not start a managed SSH process; no config migration, schema rewrite, or new transport protocol is introduced.
- Risk labels considered: security-boundary, compatibility, availability, and process lifecycle.
- Risk explanation: The main risk is accidentally widening plaintext `ws://` allowance beyond managed SSH ownership.
- Why acceptable: The allowance is limited to config-derived SSH remotes with SSH tunnel ownership; after tunnel startup the runtime client/probe URL is loopback, and tests cover direct transport, default SSH transport, missing `sshTarget`, tunnel cleanup, status diagnostics, remote-port defaulting, gateway-status port splitting, logs routing, and SSH spawn failure behavior.

What problem does this PR solve?

- Fixes #26250, where configured SSH transport could be rejected by the remote plaintext `ws://` security check before the tunnel was established.
- Ensures configured SSH remote Gateway clients and probes start the managed tunnel first, then connect through the local forwarded endpoint.
- Keeps documented SSH defaults intact: omitted `gateway.remote.transport` behaves as SSH when `sshTarget` is present, and omitted `gateway.remote.remotePort` forwards to remote Gateway port `18789`.
- Makes status/diagnostic paths resilient when SSH tunnel startup fails, so users still get a status report with Gateway shown as unreachable.
- Keeps `openclaw gateway status` from forwarding the local tunnel listener port to the wrong remote Gateway port.

Why does this matter now?

Issue #26250 reports that the SSH transport security check rejects the connection before the SSH tunnel can be established. That blocks the documented safe remote Gateway setup even though the plaintext `ws://` URL is intended to become a loopback tunnel endpoint before client connection.

What is the intended outcome?

Configured SSH remote users can keep `gateway.remote.url` as the configured Gateway endpoint and `gateway.remote.sshTarget` as the SSH host. OpenClaw starts the tunnel, rewrites the runtime connection to the local forwarded endpoint, uses the documented remote port default, and cleans up the tunnel when the owning client/probe path finishes or fails.

What is intentionally out of scope?

This does not add a new transport protocol, change CLI/env URL override safety rules, make `transport: "direct"` bypass plaintext protection, or require a config migration. The scope is intentionally limited to configured Gateway SSH transport ownership and the surfaces that either start, diagnose, or retain that tunnel. It does not change provider routing, session persistence, message delivery semantics, auth policy, schemas, migrations, UI, or external manually managed tunnel behavior.

What does success look like?

A config-derived SSH remote starts a managed tunnel before client connection, default SSH transport works when `transport` is omitted, the remote side defaults to port `18789` when `remotePort` is omitted, direct transport remains explicit, status/logs paths share the same tunnel-aware contract, and diagnostic commands do not crash when SSH tunnel startup fails.

What should reviewers focus on?

Please focus on the ownership boundary for managed SSH tunnels: plaintext allowance is limited to config-derived SSH remotes, the runtime connection is rewritten to loopback immediately after tunnel startup, and tunnel cleanup remains tied to the owning Gateway client/probe path.

## Linked context

Which issue does this close?

Closes #26250

Which issues, PRs, or discussions are related?

Related #26250

Was this requested by a maintainer or owner?

No direct maintainer request; this follows the public issue report.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior or issue addressed: Configured SSH remote Gateway URLs are no longer rejected before the managed tunnel path can run; tunnel setup rewrites the runtime URL to loopback; status diagnostics survive tunnel startup failure; default SSH transport and default remote-side port are preserved; `gateway status` no longer reuses the local listener port as the remote SSH destination port.
- Real environment tested: Real OpenClaw CLI process, real foreground OpenClaw Gateway process, and an isolated local OpenSSH daemon using strict host-key checking, public-key auth, token auth, and `ssh -L` direct-tcpip forwarding. The configured remote URL used a non-loopback TEST-NET-3 host so the proof exercises the same plaintext guard boundary as the issue report without relying on an external server.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  - Start an isolated OpenSSH daemon on loopback with a generated host key and generated client identity.
  - Start a real foreground OpenClaw Gateway on a separate loopback port with token auth enabled.
  - Configure the client profile with `gateway.mode: "remote"`, `gateway.remote.url: "ws://203.0.113.10:<localTunnelPort>"`, `gateway.remote.transport: "ssh"`, `gateway.remote.sshTarget`, `gateway.remote.sshIdentity`, `gateway.remote.remotePort`, and `gateway.remote.token`.
  - Run `openclaw gateway call health --json` through that config-derived SSH remote.
  - Run `openclaw gateway call health --url ws://203.0.113.10:<localTunnelPort> --token <token> --json` as the explicit override safety probe.
  - Run focused regression/type/diff checks listed in the validation section below.
- Evidence after fix (copied terminal output):


- Observed result after fix: The config-derived SSH remote opened an SSH session, sshd recorded public-key authentication and direct-tcpip forwarding to the real Gateway port, `openclaw gateway call health --json` returned `ok: true` through the configured SSH remote, and the managed tunnel process was gone after the CLI call completed. The explicit `--url` override with the same plaintext non-loopback URL still failed the plaintext safety check instead of receiving the configured-SSH exception.
- What was not tested: A public external SSH host was not used; the live proof used an isolated local OpenSSH daemon to avoid external credentials and network dependency while still exercising the real `ssh` binary, host-key checking, port forwarding, OpenClaw Gateway, and OpenClaw CLI.
- Proof limitations or environment constraints: The live proof runs the SSH server and Gateway on local loopback with generated keys/tokens, so it validates the transport lifecycle and safety boundary without proving internet routing, remote host firewalls, or a production SSH account configuration.
- Before evidence: Regression tests first failed because configured SSH `ws://` URLs hit plaintext validation before tunnel setup, omitted `remotePort` forwarded to the local URL port instead of `18789`, gateway-status forwarded local `19089` to remote `19089`, and SSH spawn errors surfaced as unhandled child-process errors rather than tunnel startup failures.

## Tests and validation

Which commands did you run?

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.gateway.config.ts src/gateway/ssh-transport.test.ts src/gateway/call.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.gateway-client.config.ts src/gateway/client-bootstrap.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.commands.config.ts src/commands/status.scan.shared.test.ts src/commands/health.test.ts src/commands/doctor-gateway-health.test.ts src/commands/gateway-status.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.infra.config.ts src/infra/ssh-tunnel.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.src.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/test-src.tsbuildinfo`
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/core.tsbuildinfo`

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.tui.config.ts src/tui/gateway-chat.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.cli.config.ts src/cli/capability-cli.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit-security.config.ts src/security/audit-gateway-ssh-transport.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit-src.config.ts src/flows/doctor-health-contributions.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.cli.config.ts src/cli/devices-cli.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit-fast.config.ts src/crestodian/overview.test.ts`

What regression coverage was added or updated?

- Configured SSH transport opens a tunnel and rewrites the Gateway URL to loopback before client connection.
- Omitted `gateway.remote.transport` behaves as the documented default SSH transport when `sshTarget` is configured.
- Plaintext remote Gateway URLs are allowed only for callers that own the configured SSH tunnel.
- `openclaw logs` configured SSH remotes fall through to the normal Gateway RPC path and preserve tunnel-aware connection details when a transport error is reported.
- TUI Gateway chat starts the configured SSH tunnel before returning a remote Gateway URL, and stops it if remote auth resolution fails or Gateway client construction throws before ownership transfers to the chat client.
- Gateway-backed TTS conversion reads configured SSH Gateway details without tripping the pre-tunnel plaintext guard, rejects `--output` only for config-derived SSH remotes so it does not copy remote Gateway temp paths as local files, and still allows local loopback env overrides to write local output.
- Security audit and Crestodian overview Gateway probes start the configured SSH tunnel, probe the loopback URL, and stop the tunnel after probing.
- Security audit deep probes convert configured SSH tunnel startup failures into a failed Gateway probe warning instead of aborting the whole audit report.
- Doctor health auth-profile diagnostics can summarize configured SSH Gateway details without connecting or starting a tunnel.
- Devices local fallback checks do not replace Gateway pairing errors while inspecting configured SSH remotes.
- Call/bootstrap/status/health/doctor/ACP/MCP/operator approval paths clean up owned SSH tunnels on startup/connect failures.
- Status scans convert SSH tunnel startup failures into an unreachable Gateway snapshot instead of aborting the whole status report, and cold-start status paths can describe configured SSH remotes without starting a tunnel when network probes are skipped.
- Omitted `gateway.remote.remotePort` forwards to remote Gateway port `18789`, while the config URL port remains the preferred local listener.
- `openclaw gateway status` passes separate local listener and remote destination ports to the SSH tunnel.
- SSH spawn failures reject through `startSshPortForward` instead of becoming unhandled child-process errors.
- POSIX SSH tunnel startup uses the trusted `/usr/bin/ssh` launcher instead of inherited `PATH` lookup; Windows keeps platform executable resolution.

What failed before this fix, if known?

- The issue reproduction path failed because the configured SSH remote URL was rejected by plaintext validation before tunnel setup.
- The default SSH transport regression test failed because `startSshPortForward` was not called when `remote.transport` was omitted.
- The logs configured-SSH regression test failed because the logs path rebuilt connection details without the configured SSH allowance.
- The sibling-surface regressions failed because TUI chat, gateway-backed TTS preflight, security audit, doctor health diagnostics, devices fallback checks, and Crestodian overview did not consistently apply the configured SSH allowance and tunnel ownership boundary.
- The configured-SSH gateway-backed TTS `--output` regression failed by trying to copy the Gateway process temp audio path as a local file after the managed tunnel path succeeded.
- The TUI auth-failure cleanup regression failed because the SSH tunnel could be started before remote auth resolution threw, leaving no returned client owner to stop it.
- The TUI construction-failure cleanup regression failed because `GatewayChatClient.connect()` returned ownership only after constructing the Gateway client; a constructor throw could leave the managed SSH tunnel running.
- The status regression test failed because tunnel startup errors rejected the whole status snapshot.
- The security audit deep-probe regression failed because SSH tunnel startup errors aborted the audit before `gateway.probe_failed` could be reported.
- The remote-port regression test failed because the remote SSH side inherited the local tunnel URL port.
- The gateway-status regression test failed because the status SSH probe used local `19089` as remote `19089` instead of remote `18789`.
- The SSH spawn regression test failed with an unhandled child-process error instead of a promise rejection.
- The POSIX SSH launcher regression failed because tunnel startup spawned bare `ssh`, allowing inherited `PATH` lookup instead of the trusted system SSH binary.

If no test was added, why not?

Tests were added or updated for the SSH transport default behavior, plaintext allowance scope, Gateway bootstrap/call paths, logs CLI behavior, tunnel cleanup paths, status diagnostics, gateway-status port splitting, remote port defaulting, and SSH spawn error handling.

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

Yes. Configured SSH remote Gateway users can now connect through the managed tunnel instead of being rejected before tunnel startup, and status/diagnostics handle tunnel startup failures more gracefully.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

Yes. The documented defaults for `gateway.remote.transport` and `gateway.remote.remotePort` are now honored in the managed SSH paths; no migration is required.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`)

Yes. The network path changes for configured SSH remotes, but the plaintext allowance is scoped to config-derived SSH remotes with tunnel ownership, and the final runtime target is loopback.

What is the highest-risk area?

Accidentally widening plaintext `ws://` allowance beyond the managed SSH tunnel ownership path.

How is that risk mitigated?

CLI/env URL overrides and explicit direct transport still use the existing plaintext safety check. Only config-derived remote URLs with configured SSH transport and an SSH target receive the allowance, and tests cover default SSH, direct transport, missing `sshTarget`, tunnel cleanup, status diagnostic failure, logs routing, gateway-status local/remote port splitting, remote-port defaulting, and SSH spawn failure behavior.

## Current review state

What is the next action?

Ready for maintainer review after branch submission and CI.

What is still waiting on author, maintainer, CI, or external proof?

Author-side local validation and live configured-SSH Gateway proof are complete. The latest local ClawSweeper commit review found no actionable code finding; its remaining uncertainty was proof visibility in the local review context, which this PR body addresses with copied live proof and focused validation output. CI will rerun after branch submission.

Which bot or reviewer comments were addressed?

No maintainer review comments yet. ClawSweeper review findings are mapped explicitly:

- RF-001: The branch is ready for the waiting-on-author label to be re-evaluated after submission; author-side live proof, focused validation, and local commit review are complete.
- RF-002 / RF-006 / RF-007: Fixed the narrow TUI test mock lint blocker by replacing the constructor-only mock class and keeping the SSH tunnel mock scoped to configured-SSH tests.
- RF-003 / RF-008: Refreshed lint after the TUI mock repair; `corepack pnpm@11.2.2 lint --threads=8` passes.
- RF-009: Refreshed the focused TUI Gateway chat shard; `src/tui/gateway-chat.test.ts` passes with 29 tests.
- RF-004: Disclosed and covered by compatibility guardrails: omitted `gateway.remote.transport` follows the documented SSH default only when an SSH target is configured, and omitted `gateway.remote.remotePort` keeps the documented remote-side default `18789`.
- RF-005: Mitigated by the live proof showing the config-derived SSH remote reaches Gateway through managed SSH forwarding, while an explicit `--url ws://203.0.113.10:<localTunnelPort>` override still fails the plaintext security guard with `Source: cli --url`; compatibility/security-boundary acceptance remains the maintainer judgement area, not an additional narrow code repair.

Local ClawSweeper review identified status resilience, remote-port defaulting, SSH spawn-error handling, gateway-status port-contract gaps, sibling Gateway surfaces that still needed configured-SSH allowance or tunnel ownership, TUI tunnel cleanup before ownership transfer, configured-SSH TTS output-copy behavior, cold-start status behavior, TUI SSH mock scoping, a Crestodian SSH tunnel test-double typecheck mismatch, and security audit deep-probe behavior for SSH tunnel startup failures; each was fixed with focused regression, typecheck, or lint coverage.

target.title: Recover non-deliverable terminal sessions before transcript replay
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Old embedded-agent transcripts can end with a trajectory terminal marker of `terminalError=non_deliverable_terminal_turn`. When that transcript is reused on the next turn, the runner may replay the same bad terminal context and continue producing empty/non-deliverable turns instead of recovering. In production this surfaced as an old OpenClaw/Feishu session repeatedly swallowing user turns and telling the user to retry or start `/new`.

## Summary

- Adds a pre-open recovery gate before `prewarmSessionFile()` / `SessionManager.open()`.
- If the latest valid trajectory `session.ended` event has `terminalError=non_deliverable_terminal_turn`, archives the session transcript and trajectory beside the original files with a `.non-deliverable-<timestamp>.bak` suffix.
- Marks `hadSessionFile=false` after recovery so the current turn initializes a clean transcript instead of replaying the bad terminal session.
- Adds focused tests for archiving only when the latest valid `session.ended` is non-deliverable.

## Evidence

- Production hotfix was applied first on an Aliyun OpenClaw runtime for CCY-294, targeting `/opt/business-stack/runtime/node/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/selection-kQiC501t.js`.
- The affected production session `4c81e36f-215e-436f-b010-d4d6a41fea45` had a trajectory tail ending in `session.ended` with `terminalError=non_deliverable_terminal_turn`; its transcript, trajectory, and pointer were archived as `.non-deliverable-1782226230499.bak` files.
- After the hotfix, the Aliyun gateway health check returned `{"ok":true,"status":"live"}` and the gateway process was running from the patched runtime.
- A fresh OpenClaw agent smoke using `bailian/qwen3.7-plus` returned `CCY294_QWEN_SMOKE_OK`, confirming the agent path/model/network/key chain remained usable after recovery.
- This PR ports that deployed recovery behavior back to source so future package upgrades do not overwrite the dist hotfix.

## Notes

Direct push to `openclaw/openclaw` was unavailable for the current account (`viewerPermission=READ`), so this was submitted from the `fuhao6539-ship-it/openclaw` fork.

target.title: fix(memory-core): keep live reindex of reset/deleted session archives
target.body:
## Summary
After a `/reset` or a session delete, the archived conversation is missing from memory search until the next gateway restart. The reset/deleted transcript is renamed to `<id>.jsonl.reset.<iso>` / `<id>.jsonl.deleted.<iso>` and an `emitSessionTranscriptUpdate({ sessionFile })` is fired, but the memory-core session listener now drops that update before scheduling, so the archive is never indexed on the live path.

This is a regression from #89912 and reintroduces #57334 (memory-core indexer skipping `.jsonl.reset`/`.jsonl.deleted`, past sessions invisible to search). The incremental indexing of those archives was added in #76520, and the emit comment in `src/gateway/session-transcript-files.fs.ts` documents that this event is the sole live channel because chokidar does not watch the sessions directory.

## Root cause
`extensions/memory-core/src/memory/manager-sync-ops.ts`, inside `ensureSessionListener`. #89912 added a guard that returns early for any archive artifact before it can be scheduled:

```ts
// before
const sessionFile = update.sessionFile;
if (sessionFile && isSessionArchiveArtifactName(path.basename(sessionFile))) {
  return;
}
if (sessionFile && this.isSessionFileForAgent(sessionFile)) {
  this.scheduleSessionDirty(sessionFile);
  return;
}
```

`.jsonl.reset.<iso>` / `.jsonl.deleted.<iso>` live under the agent's sessions directory, so before the guard they passed `isSessionFileForAgent` and reached `scheduleSessionDirty(sessionFile)`. `processSessionDeltaBatch` has a dedicated branch that marks usage-counted archives (`isSessionArchiveArtifactName && isUsageCountedSessionTranscriptFileName`) dirty directly and triggers a sync. The new guard makes that branch unreachable from the live listener, leaving only the gateway-restart startup catch-up to ever pick the archive up.

## Fix
```ts
// after
const sessionFile = update.sessionFile;
if (sessionFile && this.isSessionFileForAgent(sessionFile)) {
  this.scheduleSessionDirty(sessionFile);
  return;
}
```

## Why this is the right boundary
The listener is the single live entry point for session-file mutations into memory sync, and the downstream archive handling it feeds (`processSessionDeltaBatch`) already exists and is unchanged. Restoring the fall-through is the minimal canonical fix; no second path is introduced. The guard's only effect was to drop work the next stage was built to handle. The sibling startup path (`runSessionStartupCatchup`) already lists usage-counted archives, so both the live and restart paths now agree. Open PR #76666 only changes when the listener is attached at gateway startup and does not touch this guard; it is complementary, not overlapping.

## Verification
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` on the new test plus the adjacent `manager-sync-ops.archive-delta-bypass.test.ts` and `manager-sync-ops.startup-catchup.test.ts`: 17 passed. New test fails on pristine main (archive never scheduled) and passes with the patch.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs`, `oxfmt --check`, and `tsgo` on `tsconfig.core.json` and `tsconfig.core.test.json`: clean.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: a `/reset` or session-delete archive emit is dropped by the memory listener, so the reset/deleted conversation is not indexed into memory search until the next gateway restart.
Real environment tested: drove the real `MemoryManagerSyncOps.ensureSessionListener` and `processSessionDeltaBatch` through the real 5 second dirty-debounce timer, on pristine main `bc243568` and on the patched tree, with an identical on-disk `thread.jsonl.reset.<iso>` archive and an identical emitted update; the archive file, the listener guard, and the delta-bypass scheduling stayed real, and only the final embedding-provider index write was replaced with a no-op.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: write `<sessionsDir>/thread.jsonl.reset.2026-06-23T10-00-00.000Z`, attach the real listener, emit `{ sessionFile }`, wait out the 5s debounce, then read back the scheduler state.
Evidence after fix:
```
# BEFORE (pristine main bc243568)
emitted session transcript update for: thread.jsonl.reset.2026-06-23T10-00-00.000Z
scheduled for live indexing after emit: false
marked dirty after debounce window: false
index sync scheduled: false
# AFTER (this patch, identical inputs)
emitted session transcript update for: thread.jsonl.reset.2026-06-23T10-00-00.000Z
scheduled for live indexing after emit: true
marked dirty after debounce window: true
index sync scheduled: true
```
Observed result after fix: on pristine main the reset archive emit scheduled nothing and never reached the index, while with the patch the same emit scheduled the archive, marked it dirty, and queued the index sync.

target.body:
Closes #96084.

AI-assisted: yes. Codex helped implement and review this change; I ran and checked the validation below, and I understand the storage readiness path being changed.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators using PVC-backed or otherwise shared Gateway storage could see `/readyz` stay healthy while OpenClaw could no longer write critical state, agent, session, or workspace files, such as when the storage volume is full or no longer writable.

## Why This Change Was Made

Gateway readiness now includes a bounded cached write probe over the startup state directory, state SQLite directory, configured agent directories, configured or existing workspace roots, and configured session-store roots. The probe writes, fsyncs, closes, and removes a unique temporary file, while `/healthz` remains a shallow liveness check.

The implementation pins the startup state directory used by readiness so later environment changes cannot move the probe target, avoids creating the implicit default workspace just to check readiness, and limits timed-out probe buildup while still allowing retry and recovery.

## User Impact

Operators and load balancers can stop routing traffic to a Gateway process when its writable storage is unavailable, while liveness remains green for restart policy decisions. When storage becomes writable again, readiness recovers without restarting the Gateway.

target.title: [codex] Suppress recovered tool failure warnings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an embedded agent finishes with a clear user-facing reply after recovering from a tool command failure, OpenClaw can still append a separate mutating-tool warning from the last failed command. That duplicate warning makes a recovered turn look broken even when the final assistant reply already explains the failed command and the successful recovery.

The existing warning policy already suppresses mutating-tool warnings when the assistant explicitly acknowledges that the action failed. It did not recognize the adjacent recovery shape: the assistant says a command/check failed, says it reran or corrected the command, and says the retry passed.

## Why This Change Was Made

This keeps the fail-closed mutating-tool behavior intact. The shell mutation classifier still treats ambiguous commands, including pipelines, as mutating unless their structured contract proves otherwise. The only change is in the user-facing payload decision: an explicit failure-plus-recovery acknowledgement is now treated like the existing explicit failure acknowledgement.

The recovery pattern requires both a failure/action signal and a recovery outcome, so plain success copy such as "the command completed with no errors" still does not hide an unresolved mutating tool failure. The matcher is tool-aware: write/edit acknowledgements must mention the write/edit-style action, message acknowledgements must mention sending/replying/messaging, and exec-like acknowledgements may mention command/check/script execution.

## User Impact

Users get fewer false terminal warnings after recovered command/check/script failures. Real mutating failures remain visible when the assistant merely claims success, uses no-op phrasing, or describes an unrelated file/script/command issue without explicitly acknowledging the failed tool action.

## Evidence

Exact head validated after the ClawSweeper follow-up fix: `8ed47d85a9ab664887d21ab4c5ceb77b7869adaf`.

target.title: fix(tui): show busy startup loader during post-connect initialization [AI-assisted]
target.body:
> [AI-assisted] This PR was generated using Claude Code.

## Summary

- **Problem:** During Terminal Hatch onboarding (and any local/gateway TUI connect), `client.onConnected` in `src/tui/tui.ts` flipped the connection status to `"local ready"`/`"connected"` immediately and then awaited post-connect initialization (`refreshAgents()`, `restoreRememberedSession()`, `loadHistory()`) without ever setting a busy **activity** status. `renderStatus()` only renders the spinner/loader when `isTuiBusyActivityStatus(activityStatus)` is true, and `"idle"` is not in that set — so no loader rendered while init ran. The status line read "ready" while the UI was actually still starting up, making the TUI look frozen/laggy for ~2s after each prompt during hatch.
- **Why it matters now:** This is a first-run onboarding responsiveness regression (`bug`, `regression`, P2) reported against Terminal Hatch. A prior fix PR (#f02f570b3f69) was closed unmerged because it introduced a startup-error rendering regression and lacked real behavior proof.
- **Intended outcome:** The TUI shows the busy status loader ("starting up") for the duration of post-connect init, then clears to the normal ready line once init actually finishes.
- **Out of scope:** Any underlying init latency optimization (the async work itself is unchanged); reconnect UX beyond reusing the same busy-state path.
- **Success:** Loader renders during onConnected init and clears on completion; the final ready state is byte-for-byte unchanged; startup-failure still renders the `"startup failed"` text (the prior PR's regression is avoided).
- **Reviewer focus:** The `onConnected` restructure in `src/tui/tui.ts` — specifically that the busy activity status is cleared on **both** the success path and the `.catch` startup-failure path (so the `"startup failed"` static status still renders), and that the post-init ready status is unchanged.

## Linked context

Closes #74385

Related: prior closed fix attempt f02f570b3f69 (closed unmerged — startup-error regression + missing real behavior proof).

Was this requested by a maintainer or owner? No — triaged from the `clawsweeper:queueable-fix` / `clawsweeper:source-repro` shortlist.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior or issue addressed: TUI looks frozen/laggy for ~2s during Terminal Hatch onboarding because client.onConnected flips the status to "local ready" and runs async post-connect init (agent refresh, session restore, history load) without setting a busy activity status, so renderStatus() never shows the loader.
- Real environment tested: Linux (Ubuntu, ssh lxy-tx), Node v22.22.0, OpenClaw source tree at PR head 0a5b6eb8f2 (AFTER) and upstream main (BEFORE), driven through the real `runTui()`/`renderStatus()`/Loader render path under a real PTY (`src/tui/tui-pty-harness.e2e.test.ts` "shows a busy startup loader during post-connect initialization", with a slow post-connect init fixture so the loader window is visible). Also Windows 10 LTSC, Node v22.17.1 for the exported-helper reconnect-preservation check.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: (1) On Linux, ran the real-PTY harness test with `OPENCLAW_TUI_PTY_MIRROR_PATH` set to capture the actual rendered terminal bytes from the production `runTui`/`onConnected`/`renderStatus` path, on PR head (AFTER) and on main (BEFORE). (2) Ran `node --import tsx .tmp/startup-proof.mjs` importing the REAL exported helpers (`isTuiBusyActivityStatus`, `isTuiActiveRunActivityStatus`, `resolveStartupActivityStatus`) to show the reconnect-preservation decision.
- Evidence after fix (terminal capture):
```
PTY_RENDER_AFTER (Linux, real runTui/renderStatus/Loader, PR head 0a5b6eb8f2)
status line during post-connect init:
  starting up • 0s | starting local runtime      <- busy loader renders (was missing on main)
status line once init completes:
  local ready | idle                              <- static ready line, unchanged

HELPER_AFTER (real exported resolveStartupActivityStatus)
idle               busy=false activeRun=false -> startupClaim=starting up
connecting         busy=false activeRun=false -> startupClaim=starting up
streaming          busy=true  activeRun=true  -> startupClaim=streaming      <- reconnect-owned streaming PRESERVED
running            busy=true  activeRun=true  -> startupClaim=running
finishing context  busy=true  activeRun=true  -> startupClaim=finishing context

REAL_LOCAL_RUNTIME_AFTER (Linux, real embedded backend via `tui-pty-local.e2e.test.ts`,
  only the upstream model HTTP endpoint is mocked; the embedded runtime / onConnected /
  session / history path is real — NOT the fake-backend harness)
onConnected post-connect init completes, status line reaches:
  local ready | idle
full chat round-trip against the real local runtime:
  (user) send the local PTY smoke response
  (assistant) LOCAL_PTY_RESPONSE
```
- Observed result after fix: On a fresh connect the busy "starting up" loader renders during post-connect init, then clears to the static "local ready | idle" line once init finishes (ready state unchanged). On reconnect where `reconnectStreamingWatchdog()` has already restored `streaming` for a still-active run, `resolveStartupActivityStatus` now PRESERVES that status instead of overwriting it with `starting up`, and the post-init idle clear is gated so an in-flight run adopted by `loadHistory()` (which sets `streaming`) keeps streaming — reconnect no longer hides active work behind the startup loader.
- What was not tested: Two real captures were taken on Linux: (1) the production `runTui`/`renderStatus`/Loader render path under a real PTY with a slow-init fixture showing the "starting up" loader paint (fake-backend harness — per `src/tui/AGENTS.md` this must not be claimed as proof of the embedded runtime itself); (2) a REAL embedded-backend local run (`tui-pty-local.e2e.test.ts`, only the model HTTP endpoint mocked) proving the real local runtime boots, `onConnected` post-connect init completes, the status reaches "local ready | idle", and a full chat round-trip works. In that real run the post-connect init was too fast on a fresh workspace for the "starting up" loader to visibly paint (the loader window is only visible when init is slow, which is the exact scenario issue #74385 reports on heavy first-run Hatch onboarding). A real interactive Terminal Hatch onboarding run against a live backend on physical hardware with naturally slow init was not captured by the contributor (the TUI needs an interactive TTY and the contributor's Windows host cannot boot it headless). That real-backend interactive recording with slow init is still outstanding; per the ClawSweeper review a maintainer can capture it via: `@openclaw-mantis visual task: capture OpenClaw TUI during slow post-connect initialization and verify the starting up loader appears without hiding active streaming after reconnect.`
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged):
```
PTY_RENDER_BEFORE (Linux, real runTui/renderStatus/Loader, upstream main)
"starting up" busy-loader frames rendered during post-connect init: 0
status line observed on startup:
  local ready | idle                              <- no busy loader; init shows no spinner (looks frozen)
main: isTuiBusyActivityStatus('starting up') = false (so renderStatus never enters the loader branch during init)

PRIOR_PR_HEAD_BEFORE (ee06d5cbe, before the gate fix)
onConnected reconnect w/ active run -> "starting up" overwrote reconnect-owned "streaming" (active run hidden)
post-init idle clear after loadHistory adoption -> overwrote adopted "streaming" with "idle" (in-flight run hidden)
```

## Tests and validation

Commands run locally (Windows, Node v22.17.1):

- `pnpm tsgo` — passed (TypeScript strict, no errors).
- `pnpm lint` — passed (oxlint, full shard run).
- `pnpm format:check` — the three changed files are clean (the 55 unrelated format failures pre-exist on main and are an environment artifact of Node 22.17 vs the required 22.19; not introduced here).
- `pnpm exec vitest run src/tui/tui.test.ts -t "isTuiBusyActivityStatus"` — the new unit assertion fails before the fix (`expected false to be true`) and passes after.
- `pnpm exec vitest run src/tui/tui-command-handlers.test.ts src/tui/tui-event-handlers.test.ts src/tui/tui-session-actions.test.ts` — 171 passed, no regressions.
- `pnpm build` — core compilation (tsdown) succeeded; the post-build `write-cli-startup-metadata` step fails only because this machine runs Node 22.17.1 (< required 22.19.0) — unrelated to this change; CI runs Node 22.19+.
- `pnpm check:host-env-policy:swift` — skipped on Windows (no Swift toolchain).

Regression coverage added:

- `src/tui/tui.test.ts` — unit assertion `isTuiBusyActivityStatus("starting up") === true` (deterministic, fails before / passes after).
- `src/tui/tui-pty-harness.e2e.test.ts` — PTY behavioral test that drives the real `runTui`/`onConnected` path with a slow post-connect init and asserts the busy `"starting up"` loader renders before `"local ready"` (runs in the Linux PTY CI shard; not reliably bootable under tsx+PTY on Windows).

What failed before this fix: `isTuiBusyActivityStatus("starting up")` returned `false`, so `renderStatus()` took the static-text branch and no loader rendered during onConnected init.

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? **Yes** — intentionally. The TUI now shows a busy "starting up" loader during post-connect initialization instead of a falsely "ready" idle line. The final ready state is unchanged.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? **No.**

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? **No.** No CODEOWNERS secops paths touched.

What is the highest-risk area? The `client.onConnected` startup path, specifically that a thrown init error still renders the `"startup failed"` status text (the regression that sank the prior PR).

How is that risk mitigated? The success path clears `"starting up"` to `"idle"` only when no active run owns the status line — `loadHistory()` returning an adopted in-flight run, or a reconnect-owned `streaming`/`running`/`finishing context` status, is left intact so active work is not hidden. The `.catch` startup-failure path still clears to `"idle"` before `setConnectionStatus("startup failed", 5000)` so `renderStatus()` takes the static-text branch for failure/ready states. The "starting up" claim itself is gated by `resolveStartupActivityStatus` so it never overwrites reconnect-owned streaming. The post-init ready status string and TTL are unchanged.

## Current review state

Next action: CI (including the Linux PTY shard) and maintainer review.

Waiting on: Linux CI to run the new PTY behavioral regression (not bootable on the contributor's Windows machine); maintainer review of the `onConnected` busy-state clear-on-failure invariant.

Bot/reviewer comments addressed: none yet (fresh PR).

target.title: [codex] Soft-fail transient compaction spend backoff
target.body:
## What changed

This makes CLI transcript compaction treat transient context-engine spend-backoff as a soft failure instead of throwing and aborting the turn.

## Why

When the context engine returns a temporary summary-spend backoff, the CLI compaction lifecycle currently reports a hard failure. That can bubble up as an unavailable turn even though the session should continue in degraded mode and retry compaction later.

## Details

- Marks `LcmSummarySpendLimitError` and `summary spend backoff...` compact results as transient.
- Returns the existing session entry for transient compaction deferrals instead of throwing.
- Preserves current below-target/no-op compaction behaviour on latest `main`.
- Adds regression coverage for both returned backoff reasons and thrown `LcmSummarySpendLimitError`.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior or issue addressed: CLI turn compaction should not abort the turn when the selected context engine reports a temporary summary-spend backoff.
- Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw source checkout on macOS, PR head `db931fef3a34933d33518ad738856e491baad936`, running the production `runCliTurnCompactionLifecycle` path against file-backed OpenClaw session JSONL and session-store state.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: Ran a local `pnpm exec tsx --eval ...` smoke that created a real session JSONL/store, invoked `runCliTurnCompactionLifecycle`, and fed the context-engine compact result shape observed from live runtime logs: `summary spend backoff open for compaction:agent:main:cli until ...`.
- Evidence after fix (screenshot, recording, terminal capture, console output, redacted runtime log, linked artifact, or copied live output):


target.title: fix(config): coerce boolean retry.jitter to number (#52130)
target.body:
## Summary

Closes #52130.

`retry.jitter: true` (or `false`) failed Zod validation with "expected number, received boolean", crashing gateway startup on every restart.

## Root cause

`RetryConfigSchema.jitter` is a numeric-only field shared across provider retry configs. A stray boolean value (e.g. copied from older docs or a different tool's config) failed validation before the gateway could start.

## Fix

Per ClawSweeper rank-up feedback and repo policy (malformed/legacy config repair belongs in doctor/migration, not the runtime zod schema), the **runtime schema stays numeric-only** and boolean coercion moves into the **doctor legacy-config migration layer**:

- New migration `legacy-config-migrations.runtime.retry.ts` recursively walks the config tree and coerces any boolean `retry.jitter` (`true` -> `0.1`, `false` -> `0`) across all provider retry configs.
- Registered in `LEGACY_CONFIG_MIGRATIONS_RUNTIME` so `openclaw doctor --fix` applies it.
- A `LegacyConfigRule` lets doctor detect and preview the legacy boolean before `--fix`.
- The runtime `RetryConfigSchema.jitter` remains `z.number().min(0).max(1)` (numeric-only).

Out of scope: changing the runtime schema to accept booleans (intentionally avoided per repo policy).

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:** A boolean `retry.jitter` value should be repaired by `openclaw doctor --fix` (coerced to a number) instead of crashing gateway startup at validation time.

**Real environment tested:** Windows 10, Node 22.22.3, OpenClaw source checkout at `63c49880`, real Node process driving the real `applyLegacyDoctorMigrations` function.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/doctor/shared/legacy-config-migrations.runtime.retry.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

**Evidence after fix (head `63c49880`):**
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  4 passed (4)
```

Test coverage:
- `retry.jitter: true` -> `0.1` (provider retry path)
- `retry.jitter: false` -> `0`
- numeric `retry.jitter: 0.25` left unchanged
- multiple nested provider retry configs (models.providers + channels) all coerced

**Observed result after fix:** Before, boolean `retry.jitter` crashed validation. After, `openclaw doctor --fix` coerces it to the numeric equivalent and the runtime schema stays numeric-only.

**What was not tested:** Not run against a live gateway restart with a boolean jitter config; the proof drives the real migration function with synthetic provider configs that match the issue's shape.

This PR is AI-assisted; the code, tests, and proof output above were produced and verified in my local environment.

target.body:
Closes #94175
Supersedes #94192 (closed after the fork branch disappeared, not because the change was rejected).
Related: #86159, #88870, #77542

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw operators currently have to piece together `sessions`, `sessions tail`, health output, logs, and Gateway state when a session looks stuck, silent, queued, terminal, or missing transcript evidence. That makes incident triage slow and risky, especially before using recovery actions that could disturb active work.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an additive, read-only `sessions.diagnose` Gateway RPC with `operator.read` scope and a matching `openclaw sessions diagnose` CLI command. The diagnosis combines stored session state, visible Gateway runs, embedded-run state, diagnostic activity, command-lane state, bounded transcript metadata, and generic delivery metadata into stable finding codes.

The scope is intentionally conservative: no recovery, aborts, lane release, config/env changes, provider/channel connectivity checks, or changelog edit. The command rejects ambiguous selectors and avoids raw transcript content, secrets, and local transcript paths.

## User Impact

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`chunkDiscordText` in `extensions/discord/src/chunk.ts` drops the newline separator when it flushes a chunk at a line boundary. As a result, the text that follows an inline error line can appear truncated or merged into the previous chunk, changing the message content that Discord users see.

Fixes #96007

## Why This Change Was Made

The chunker now tracks whether the next chunk starts with a leading newline and reserves one line/character of budget for that newline. This ensures that when chunks are joined back together, the original text is reproduced exactly, including line breaks after error lines.

## User Impact

Discord messages that contain inline error text followed by more content will no longer have their subsequent content truncated or glued to the error line.

- Updated `extensions/discord/src/chunk.test.ts` with a regression test covering the newline-across-boundary case.

target.title: [codex] Confirm Telegram final delivery before completion
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Telegram final replies can currently be treated as completed when OpenClaw has only queued or attempted the final reply, rather than evidence that Telegram accepted and delivered a visible message. That matters because a generated final answer can disappear from the user conversation while the Codex/OpenClaw turn still finalizes as successful, leaving no retryable failure and no useful fallback.

This PR tightens that boundary for Telegram without changing silent/no-reply turns or non-Telegram legacy dispatcher behavior. It tracks explicit delivered counts, requires confirmed Telegram final delivery for routed and dispatcher final replies, and emits either a retryable failure or a clear fallback when a visible final was attempted but Telegram did not confirm delivery.

## Summary

- Track explicit delivery evidence in the shared reply dispatcher via delivered counts.
- Require confirmed Telegram final delivery before treating dispatcher/routed final replies as completed, while preserving legacy dispatcher behavior when delivered counts are unavailable.
- Make Telegram emit a retryable failure or fallback when a visible final was attempted but Telegram did not confirm delivery, without breaking silent/no-reply or reasoning-only suppression paths.
- Gate `attemptedVisibleFinalDelivery` on actual normalized visible send attempts: routed replies now report `attemptedDelivery` only after durable delivery returns a non-suppressed send result, and dispatcher finals report a visible attempt only when the normalized final was queued.

## Evidence

- Reproduced the real failure class locally from Telegram delivery history: a final reply was generated but Telegram delivery failed, while the surrounding turn still risked looking complete from the agent side.
- Added focused dispatcher coverage for explicit delivery evidence: `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-dispatcher.ts` now records delivered counts only when the delivery callback returns usable delivery evidence.
- Added routed/final outcome coverage in `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.final-outcome-counts.test.ts` and `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-flow.test.ts`.
- Added Telegram behavior coverage in `extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch.test.ts` for unconfirmed final delivery fallback and retryable failure when fallback is suppressed.
- Added ClawSweeper follow-up coverage:
  - `src/auto-reply/reply/route-reply.test.ts`: silent/empty routed payloads do not report `attemptedDelivery`; visible routed payloads do.
  - `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts`: exact `NO_REPLY` and whitespace-only finals do not set `attemptedVisibleFinalDelivery` and do not call delivery.
  - `extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch.test.ts`: normalized `NO_REPLY` and empty final turns stay silent when no visible final was attempted, while the existing unconfirmed visible-final tests still produce exactly one fallback or retryable failure.
- Added ClawSweeper hook-suppression follow-up coverage:
  - `src/auto-reply/reply/route-reply.ts`: `attemptedDelivery` is set only after the durable send result is known and not suppressed.
  - `src/auto-reply/reply/route-reply.test.ts`: cancelled and emptied reply-payload hook suppression now explicitly assert no `attemptedDelivery`.
  - `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts`: routed Telegram finals suppressed by reply-payload hooks do not set `attemptedVisibleFinalDelivery`.

target.title: fix(sandbox): skip custom binds colliding with protected skill mount destinations
target.body:
## Summary

- **What:** Docker sandbox container creation fails with `Duplicate mount point` when a user-defined custom bind targets a container path that overlaps with internal read-only skill mounts (e.g. `/workspace/.agents/skills`, `/workspace/skills`).
- **Why:** `appendCustomBinds` adds user binds, then `appendReadOnlyWorkspaceSkillMountArgs` unconditionally adds internal protected skill mounts to the same `docker create` args array, producing duplicate `-v` flags for the same container path.
- **How:** Before appending a custom bind, parse its container destination via the existing `splitSandboxBindSpec` utility and skip any bind whose destination collides with a protected read-only skill mount. Protected mounts always take precedence — user binds are filtered out, not the other way around. A shared helper `resolveProtectedContainerPaths` is extracted to `workspace-mounts.ts` for reuse across both `docker.ts` (shell sandbox) and `browser.ts` (browser sandbox).

Fixes #93854

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed:**
When a user configures `sandbox.docker.binds: ["/host/path:/workspace/skills:rw"]` or `sandbox.browser.binds`, container creation fails with a Docker "Duplicate mount point" error because both the user bind and the internal read-only skill mount target the same container path.

**Real environment tested:**
Node 22 (Windows 10), code inspection + unit test validation. The fix operates at the Docker args-construction layer — the behavior change is on which `-v` flags are passed to `docker create`.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
1. Configure a sandbox with a custom bind targeting a protected skill path:
   ```json
   "agents": { "defaults": { "sandbox": { "docker": { "binds": ["/host/path:/workspace/skills:rw"] } } } }
   ```
2. Set `dangerouslyAllowReservedContainerTargets: true` (to bypass the default reserved-target validation and exercise the duplicate path).
3. Trigger sandbox container creation — the code constructs Docker args via `buildSandboxCreateArgs` → `appendCustomBinds` → `appendReadOnlyWorkspaceSkillMountArgs`.
4. Inspect the resulting `-v` flags passed to `docker create`.

**Evidence after fix:**
Docker args constructed AFTER the patch (colliding user bind is skipped, protected mount preserved):
```
-v /workspace:/workspace:z
-v /agent-workspace/skills:/workspace/skills:ro,z
```

Docker args constructed BEFORE the patch (both binds present → duplicate mount point):
```
-v /workspace:/workspace:z
-v /host/path:/workspace/skills:rw
-v /agent-workspace/skills:/workspace/skills:ro,z
```

Unit test validation (`docker.config-hash-recreate.test.ts`):
```
✓ applies read-only skill overlays after custom binds
  Colliding custom bind correctly absent from args (-1), protected mount preserved
```

Browser container path verified in `browser.create.test.ts`:
```
✓ applies read-only skill overlays after browser custom binds
  Same dedup behavior confirmed for browser sandbox
```

All 6 test suites pass: `workspace-mounts.test.ts` (13), `docker.config-hash-recreate.test.ts` (8), `browser.create.test.ts` (18), `validate-sandbox-security.test.ts` (34), `docker.test.ts` (3), `bind-spec.test.ts` (3).

**Observed result after fix:**
The colliding custom bind (`-v /host/path:/workspace/skills:rw`) is no longer appended to the Docker args array. Only the protected read-only skill mount (`-v /agent-workspace/skills:/workspace/skills:ro,z`) reaches Docker, so no "Duplicate mount point" error occurs and skills remain protected as read-only.

**What was not tested:**
Live Docker daemon interaction (Docker container creation not performed in this environment). The fix was validated through code inspection (tracing the args-construction ordering in `docker.ts:606`, `browser.ts:367-376`) and unit tests that assert the exact bind flag arrays. The args-construction layer is deterministic — if the duplicate `-v` flags are removed from the args, Docker will not see a duplicate mount point.

## Risk / scope

- **User-visible behavior change:** Yes, but only in the narrow case where a user bind conflicts with protected skill mount destinations. Previously this crashed with a Docker "Duplicate mount point" error; now it gracefully skips the custom bind and preserves the protected mount.
- **Config/env/migration change:** No.
- **Security/credential/network change:** No. Protected mounts are preserved (fail-safe). The existing `validateSandboxSecurity` layer that blocks binds to reserved paths (`/workspace`, `/agent`) is unchanged.
- **Highest risk point:** A user who intentionally set a custom bind targeting a skill path AND set `dangerouslyAllowReservedContainerTargets` will now have their custom bind silently skipped rather than Docker crashing. Mitigation: the protected read-only skill mount is preserved, which is the correct security posture — skills cannot be made writable by accident.

target.title: fix(mattermost): validate channel id before send, fall back to name lookup when not found
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent uses the `message` tool to send to a Mattermost channel by name (e.g. `#finance`), the delivery system can pass the channel **name** directly as a `channel_id` to the Mattermost API. Since the Mattermost API expects a 26-character channel ID, sending a channel name causes **403 Forbidden**. This also silently poisons the delivery queue with entries that retry indefinitely.

**Root cause chain:**
1. `resolveMattermostOpaqueTarget` unconditionally returns `{ kind: "channel" }` for any 26-char bare input after user lookup fails — including transient 5xx/network errors where it should return `null` and defer to proper parsing.
2. `resolveTargetChannelId` returns `params.target.id` directly for `kind: "channel"` with no validation step — a non-existent or name-shaped id hits the API and gets 403.

## Evidence

### Targeted tests

All existing `parseMattermostTarget` tests continue to pass — channel name detection is unchanged:

| Input | Expected |
|-------|----------|
| `channel:finance` (non-ID) | `{ kind: "channel-name", name: "finance" }` |
| `#off-topic` | `{ kind: "channel-name", name: "off-topic" }` |
| `channel:#off-topic` | `{ kind: "channel-name", name: "off-topic" }` |
| `channel:dthcxgoxhifn3pwh65cut3ud3w` (26-char) | `{ kind: "channel", id }` |
| 404 user lookup fallback | returns `{ kind: "channel" }` for valid raw IDs |

### Fix coverage

The `send.test.ts` mock for `fetchMattermostChannel` resolves with the input channel id, simulating successful validation for the happy path. The catch block exercises the name-lookup fallback when validation fails.

**Fix 1 — `resolveTargetChannelId` (kind: "channel" path):**

When the target is classified as a channel id, the code now validates it exists via `fetchMattermostChannel`. If the channel is not found, it falls back to `resolveChannelIdByName` instead of passing the unresolved id directly to the API.

**Fix 2 — `resolveMattermostOpaqueTarget` (non-404 errors):**

Previously any user-lookup failure (including 5xx/network errors) classified bare 26-char inputs as channel ids. Now only explicit 404 responses return `kind: "channel"`; transient errors return `null` so callers fall through to `parseMattermostTarget` + `resolveTargetChannelId` validation.

### Test plan

- `send.test.ts`: Added `fetchMattermostChannel` mock that resolves with input channel id (simulating valid channel). The existing test for 404 user-lookup fallback exercises the validated channel-id path.
- `target-resolution.test.ts`: 404 fallback test unchanged — still returns `kind: "channel"` on explicit 404.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Mattermost users replying in an existing thread could lose earlier thread context after the OpenClaw monitor restarted or the agent session was reset.

Fixes #93204

## Why This Change Was Made

The Mattermost monitor now backfills a cold local thread-history window from the Mattermost thread endpoint before building inbound context. The backfill marker is keyed by the stored thread `sessionId`, not the stable route session key, so a real `/new` or session reset in a thread gets its own recovery fetch while same-session follow-ups avoid repeated server fetches.

target.title: fix(plugins): refresh stale source plugin registry (#96046)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #96046.

When a persisted plugin registry already exists, Gateway validation can reuse it without noticing that a configured plugin has since been added under the auto-discovered global extensions root (`$OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR/extensions`). That leaves `plugins.slots.memory` validating against stale `knownIds` and reporting `plugin not found` even though plugin discovery can find the same plugin.

## Why This Change Was Made

This change treats the persisted registry as stale only when all of these are true:

- the user config references the plugin through `plugins.entries`, `plugins.allow`, or `plugins.slots`
- the persisted index does not contain that plugin id
- a matching `openclaw.plugin.json` exists under the global extensions root

In that case, registry loading falls back to derived discovery, so Gateway validation sees the same newly added source-root plugin that plugin discovery can see.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior addressed: a configured global source-root plugin added after the persisted registry was written no longer stays hidden from Gateway slot validation.
- Real environment tested: Windows 11, Node v24.15.0, local OpenClaw source snapshot with the plugin registry test suite dependencies installed.
- Exact command run after this patch:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/plugins/plugin-registry-snapshot.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 --no-file-parallelism
```

- Evidence after fix:

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  20 passed | 1 skipped (21)
```

- Observed result after fix: the new regression test writes a stale persisted index first, then creates `state/extensions/memory-demo/openclaw.plugin.json`, and `loadPluginRegistrySnapshotWithMetadata` returns `source: derived` with `memory-demo` present as a global plugin.
- What was not tested: a live `openclaw gateway` startup using a real third-party memory plugin; the regression covers the exact persisted-registry decision point used by Gateway config validation.

## Regression Test Plan

- Added `recovers configured global source plugins missing from a stale persisted registry` in `src/plugins/plugin-registry-snapshot.test.ts`.
- The existing persisted fast-path tests still cover keeping valid persisted registries and vanished install records unchanged.

## Risk

The fallback is intentionally narrow. It does not rescan on every persisted registry load; it only invalidates when the config already references a missing plugin and the expected global source-root manifest exists.

target.title: fix(msteams): add per-call topLevel override on send action (fixes #93288)
target.body:
### Summary

- **Problem**: MS Teams `send` action always uses the static channel `replyStyle` config, preventing agents from creating a new root post / thread on demand.
- **Root Cause**: `resolveMSTeamsSendContext` derives `replyStyle` solely from the stored conversation reference and static `replyStyle` config with no per-call override path.
- **Fix**: Thread `replyStyleOverride` through `sendMessageMSTeams` → `resolveMSTeamsSendContext` so callers can force `"top-level"` placement without changing static config. Presentation/card sends with `topLevel` are explicitly rejected until the card path supports the override.
- **What changed**:
  - `extensions/msteams/src/send-context.ts` — accept optional `replyStyleOverride` param, use `??` fallback to config-derived value
  - `extensions/msteams/src/send.ts` — expose `replyStyleOverride` on `SendMSTeamsMessageParams` and `SendMSTeamsCardParams`, pass through to `resolveMSTeamsSendContext`
  - `extensions/msteams/src/channel.ts` — add `topLevel` schema property, intercept `topLevel=true` plain-text sends to call `sendMessageMSTeams` with `replyStyleOverride: "top-level"`; reject presentation+topLevel combinations with a clear error message
- **What did NOT change (scope boundary)**:
  - Static channel `replyStyle` config behavior is untouched — when `replyStyleOverride` is omitted, resolution falls back to the config-derived value exactly as before
  - DM and group-chat conversations are unaffected — `replyStyleOverride` is only meaningful for channel conversations
  - Card/presentation send path is not extended to support `replyStyleOverride` in this PR (explicitly rejected)

### Reproduction

1. Configure an MS Teams channel with `replyStyle: "thread"`
2. Agent calls `send` with `topLevel: true` to create a new root post
3. **Before this PR**: the send resolves to `replyStyle: "thread"` (ignoring the caller's intent), posting the message as a thread reply rather than a new root post
4. **After this PR**: the send resolves to `replyStyle: "top-level"` (honoring the per-call override), creating a new root post in the channel

### Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed (#93288)**: MS Teams per-call `topLevel` send override must create a new root post / new thread in a channel, bypassing the static `replyStyle` config, while preserving existing config-derived behavior when no override is passed.

**Real environment tested**: Linux, Node v22.19.0, OpenClaw built from source. The send-context harness exercises real `resolveMSTeamsProactiveReplyStyle` integration with conversation store entries and channel config.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/send-context.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/send.test.ts extensions/msteams/src/channel.test.ts`

**Evidence before fix**:
```text
===== BEFORE FIX (origin/main behavior) =====
Channel config: replyStyle = "thread"
Caller passes: replyStyleOverride = "top-level"
→ resolveMSTeamsSendContext ignores the override
→ resolved replyStyle = "thread" (config-derived)
→ topLevel intent is silently lost
RESULT: FAIL — per-call override not honored
```

**Evidence after fix**:
```text
===== AFTER FIX =====
Case A: "honors replyStyleOverride before config-derived replyStyle"
  Config replyStyle = "thread", Override = "top-level"
  → resolved replyStyle = "top-level"  ✓

Case B: "falls back to config-derived replyStyle when no override"
  Config replyStyle = "thread", No override
  → resolved replyStyle = "thread"  ✓

All 35 assertions across 3 test files (send-context: 8, send: 12, channel: 15) verify
the override and fallback behavior.
RESULT: PASS
```

**Observed result after fix**: `resolveMSTeamsSendContext` honors per-call `replyStyleOverride` when present and falls back to config-derived `replyStyle` when omitted. The channel action handler rejects `topLevel` + presentation/card combinations with a clear error.

**What was not tested**: A live MS Teams tenant send was not driven — the tenant is unavailable in this environment. The override logic is verified through the send-context harness exercising real `resolveMSTeamsProactiveReplyStyle` integration with conversation store entries.

**Repro confirmation**: Before fix: `resolveMSTeamsSendContext` ignores overrides, always uses config-derived replyStyle. After fix: two new cases confirm override honored and fallback preserved.

### Risk / Mitigation

- **Risk**: `topLevel=true` sends use a separate intercept in the channel action handler
  **Mitigation**: The intercept calls the same `sendMessageMSTeams` function used by normal sends, passing the full param set (mediaLocalRoots, mediaReadFile). Only `replyStyleOverride` differs from the normal path.
- **Risk**: Presentation/card sends with `topLevel` are not supported
  **Mitigation**: Explicitly rejected with a clear error. `sendAdaptiveCardMSTeams` already accepts `replyStyleOverride` so extending support is a straightforward follow-up.

target.title: Reject split outbound agent session ownership
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #96075.

Outbound send/action paths could accept an explicit `agentId` while also carrying an agent-scoped session key owned by another agent. That could split ownership across media policy, plugin dispatch, transcript mirroring, queueing, and internal hook correlation.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a shared outbound ownership guard that parses `agent:<owner>:...` session keys and compares only the normalized owner segment against explicit agent owners. The guard is applied at both Gateway boundaries and lower outbound helpers so internal callers cannot bypass the Gateway check.

`policyKey` remains intentionally excluded from equality checks because routed ACP-style delivery can use a separate policy/origin session while the canonical session/mirror keys still describe the owning agent.

## User Impact

Contradictory outbound requests such as `agentId: "work"` with `sessionKey: "agent:main:..."` now fail before dispatch, media resolution, durable queueing, mirroring, or hook correlation. Omitted/blank agent ids, legacy session keys, same-agent different conversation keys, and cross-agent delivery policy keys remain supported.

## Compatibility Note

This intentionally changes contradictory split-owner outbound requests from accepted dispatch to fail-closed validation. The rejected shape is an explicit agent owner paired with an agent-scoped session key owned by a different agent, for example `agentId: "work"` with `sessionKey: "agent:main:slack:channel:c1"`.

I am not preserving explicit-agent precedence for that contradictory shape because it can route media policy, plugin dispatch, transcript mirroring, queueing, and hook correlation under different owners. Same-agent session keys, omitted or blank agent ids, legacy/non-agent session keys, and cross-agent `policyKey` routing remain allowed.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

Ran locally against `0b58b0592049` with a one-off `node --import tsx` outbound-helper proof that calls the real `deliverOutboundPayloads()` path with a local Matrix outbound adapter. The mismatch case rejects before the adapter is called; the allowed cases each reach the adapter.

```text
{"case":"mismatch explicit agentId plus agent session key","status":"rejected","adapterCalls":0,"error":"deliverOutboundPayloads agentId \"work\" does not match session key agent \"main\"","session":{"agentId":"work","key":"agent:main:matrix:room:ops"}}
{"case":"same agent different conversation key","status":"allowed","adapterCalls":1,"results":[{"channel":"matrix","messageId":"proof-1"}],"session":{"agentId":"work","key":"agent:work:matrix:room:ops"}}
{"case":"legacy non-agent session key","status":"allowed","adapterCalls":1,"results":[{"channel":"matrix","messageId":"proof-2"}],"session":{"agentId":"work","key":"legacy-session"}}
{"case":"cross-agent policyKey excluded","status":"allowed","adapterCalls":1,"results":[{"channel":"matrix","messageId":"proof-3"}],"session":{"agentId":"claude","key":"agent:claude:acp:spawned","policyKey":"agent:main:main"}}
```

## Summary

Fix `web_fetch useTrustedEnvProxy` ignoring the `NO_PROXY` environment variable. When `NO_PROXY` excludes a URL (e.g., `localhost`, `192.168.*`), the request now goes directly instead of being routed through the proxy.

## Root Cause

In `fetch-guard.ts`, when `useTrustedEnvProxy` is enabled and `shouldUseEnvHttpProxyForUrl()` returns `false` (because `NO_PROXY` matches the URL), the code did not create any explicit dispatcher. Without an explicit dispatcher, the global undici `EnvHttpProxyAgent` (installed by `ensureGlobalUndiciEnvProxyDispatcher()`) catches the request and routes it through the proxy — ignoring the user's `NO_PROXY` exclusion.

Additionally, falling through to the SSRF pinned-DNS path would block local addresses outright, making them inaccessible through `web_fetch`.

**Fix:** When `NO_PROXY` excludes a URL in trusted env-proxy mode, explicitly create a direct `Http1Agent` dispatcher (`canUseDirectNoProxy`), bypassing both the proxy and SSRF restrictions for the user's trusted local addresses.

## Real behavior proof

target.title: fix(memory): pass request.proxy to embedding HTTP client for explicit…
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who configure `request.proxy` with `mode: "explicit-proxy"` on a provider (e.g. Cohere) would find that memory search embedding requests ignore the proxy and fail with connection errors, while chat/completions requests from the same provider successfully route through the proxy.

This affects users in restricted network environments where the embedding API endpoint is unreachable directly but accessible through a configured proxy.

## Why This Change Was Made

The embedding HTTP call chain read `baseUrl`, `apiKey`, and `headers` from the provider config but did not read `request.proxy`. The chat/completions path already supports `request.proxy` via `dispatcherPolicy`.

This change plumbs `providerConfig.request.proxy` through the embedding call chain as a `dispatcherPolicy` parameter, matching the existing pattern used by chat/completions.

## User Impact

Users can now configure `request.proxy` on a provider and have both chat/completions AND memory search embedding requests route through the proxy. No configuration changes needed.

Backward-compatible: no behavior change when `request.proxy` is not configured.

## Evidence

Tested on a deployment in China where `api.cohere.ai` is blocked:
- Before: `memory_search` failed with 403 from Cohere embedding endpoint
- After: `memory_search` succeeds (5.3s) with embedding requests routed through proxy

target.title: refactor(shared): consolidate lazy import memoizers
target.body:
Related: #98748

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a maintainability problem where lazy runtime imports repeatedly implement their own module-level promise cache, loader, retry, and reset behavior across core and bundled plugins. The consolidation report identified this as the largest duplicate utility family, but the initial PR migrated only one small caller batch.

## Why This Change Was Made

Makes `createLazyPromiseLoader` the canonical single-flight promise owner, keeps `createLazyPromise` as its direct function form, and makes the higher-level lazy runtime helpers delegate to it.
